**Settled (Patrick, 2026-10-07).** (1) “Facets” is the book's one image: love is multifaceted, like a diamond, one thing seen from different angles. Every part of the definition is a facet of the one love. ### 129. The open hand — re-examine the metaphor for faith, and find a closer one (book-wide)

*Opened 2026-10-01 at Patrick's request, during the Ch. 10 bishop-readiness pass.*

**The task, in his words:** re-evaluate the open-hand metaphor. The Reformed use this image, and it is not quite what we mean by faith. We mean the submission of the intellect and the will to the goodness, truth and beauty of God, to His love. We probably need another metaphor that is closer.

**Why it matters.** In Reformed teaching the “empty hand” is faith as the bare instrument that receives a righteousness credited from outside, and adds nothing. The Church's definition is different: “By faith, man completely submits his intellect and his will to God” (CCC 143; Dei Verbum 5, “the full submission of intellect and will”). Faith is a whole person's free yes, moved first by grace (CCC 153–155), and it works through love (Gal 5:6). An image of a passive, empty hand can carry the other theology in with it.

**Scope (counted 2026-10-01, raw; read each in context before changing anything).** Chapter 9 owns the image: “The Open Hand: We Cannot Receive What We Refuse to Give” and the closed fist / clenched heart passages (§8 Closed-Fist rewrite; entries 107, 108, 114). Counts: “open hand” 12 (Chs. 9, 10); “closed fist” 6 (Chs. 9, 17); “clenched” 4 (Ch. 9); “empty-handed” 2 (Chs. 9, 10); “open our hands” 2 (Chs. 9, 10). Ch. 10 Redline 1 (pending) itself proposes “comes to Him with empty hands” (line 215) and “let Him open our hands” (line 197); both should wait for this todo rather than add to the image.

**Settle first.** (1) Where the hand stands for *sacrifice* (giving, letting go, the closed fist of selfishness), it may be fine; §2 lists “open hand / closed fist” as Patrick's controlling metaphor for sacrifice. Where it stands for *faith* (receiving salvation), it is the Reformed image. Sort each use by which it means. (2) Candidate images that carry intellect and will, freely given, for Patrick to choose among: the disciple at the Teacher's feet (Ch. 9 already has the section; cf. Luke 10:39); the bowed head and bent knee (cf. Phil 2:10–11); the bride's “I do” (Ch. 10's Amen); Mary's *Fiat* (Luke 1:38); the obedience of faith, *ob-audire*, hearing (CCC 144, already in Ch. 9). Keep the grace-first rule: God moves first, our free yes receives.

**Method.** Read, don't sweep: inventory every use, sort sacrifice from faith against the chapter text, propose the replacement image, then one redline per chapter (Ch. 9 first).

### 61. Divine simplicity — the four are one in God, never “parts” of Him (book-wide review)

*Opened 2026-09-25 at Patrick's request.*

The task, in his words: we say truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice are bound in love, which is to say they are integral to God's nature and essence. They are not “parts of God” but one with Him. Review the book so that nothing describes them as if they were parts, which would go against divine simplicity.

**The doctrine, stated precisely** (so the review works from the Church's terms rather than ours). God is “one essence, substance or nature entirely simple” (Lateran IV, in CCC 202). He has no parts and no qualities added to His being; His truth, His justice and His mercy are each identical with His essence and so with one another (ST I q.3 aa.6–7). We still rightly speak of them one at a time, because we know God through creatures and so need many names for one reality. The names are not synonyms, but what they name in God is one (ST I q.13 a.4). The better word for Patrick's “homogenous” is *identical with His essence*: in God, justice is not something He has but what He is (see the Ch. 7 answer, 2026-09-24: no verse says “God is justice,” but simplicity makes it true).

**Three cautions to settle before editing.**

\(1\) *Sacrifice is not said of the divine essence in the same way as the other three.* Within the Trinity there is total self-gift but no loss; sacrifice is what that self-gift becomes when it enters a fallen world, supremely at the Cross. Ch. 3:133 already says exactly this (“when that self-giving enters a fallen world, it takes the form of the Cross”). The review must not overcorrect into “sacrifice is God's essence.” This is the same question as todo 44 (sacrifice and self-gift). Settle the two together.

\(2\) *Mercy in God is not an emotion.* It is His goodness as it lifts up misery, attributed to Him in its effect, not as a passion He undergoes (ST I q.21 a.3). Watch for any sentence that gives God a changing feeling.

\(3\) *Keep the line between God and us.* In human love the four really are distinct virtues and really can be torn apart. That is the whole Binding Check and “When the Thread Is Cut” framework, and it is right. The review targets only sentences about God's own nature, not the diagnostics of human love. The canonical definition describes love as given in covenant, and it is not in question.

**What to look for.** Language that, said of God, implies composition: “parts,” “components,” “ingredients,” “anatomy,” “made up of,” “God has four …”; pillars ranked or weighed within God; one attribute limiting or balancing another in Him (“His justice restrains His mercy”); and §1's own “no pillar is metaphysically prior,” which is true but should rest on simplicity, not on four things standing level. Scope counted 2026-09-25 (raw, unsorted, so most will be about human love and fine): “four pillars” 24 in Chs. 5, 9–14; “four threads” 10 in Chs. 5, 9, 10, 14; “component” 22 in Chs. 15–17; “anatomy” in Chs. 5 and 15; “ingredient” in the Introduction and Ch. 10; “parts of” once in Ch. 8. Also check Ch. 8's “Justice and Mercy in One Divine Nature” section (§7), Ch. 3's “God IS love” passage (line 143), Ch. 5's Aquinas integration, and the Introduction's display of the definition.

**Possible positive addition.** One staging passage, once, in Ch. 3 or Ch. 5 (the entry 38 method): in God the four are not four things but one; we name them one at a time because that is how creatures come to know Him (ST I q.13 a.4). Every later chapter can then treat one thread without implying a part. The only mention of simplicity now is Ch. 5's Further Study line on Aquinas.

**Method.** Read, don't sweep. Sort each hit by whether it speaks of God or of us, against the chapter text (see the entry 37 warning), then redline.

### 45. “To will good to another” — retranslating the Aquinas definition

**✅ Settled 2026-09-29 — see entry 89** (“to will the good for another”; *amare* fixed; no credit to Aristotle, no claim Aquinas coined it). Move to Completed at the next tidy.

*Opened 2026-09-19 at Patrick's request.*

**The task, in his words:** consider using “love is to will good to another” instead of “willing the good of another” — a more literal translation, closer to what is meant by it, and one that makes more sense in the light of the book's definition.

**The Latin supports him.** Latin has no article, so “*the* good” is a translator's addition, and *alicui* is a dative — good willed *to* someone, not the good *of* someone. “To will good to another” is the literal rendering.

⚠ **Found while opening this todo — a real error to fix as part of it.** `chapter_05.md:67` gives the Latin as *amor est velle alicui bonum*. Aquinas's text is ***amare* est velle alicui bonum** — the infinitive “to love,” not the noun “love” (ST I-II q.26 a.4, respondeo, verified at corpusthomisticum.org). The correct Latin reads literally “*to love* is to will good to someone,” which is exactly Patrick's rendering. Also: Thomas attributes the line to Aristotle (“sicut Philosophus dicit in II Rhetoric.”), while line 67 calls it “St. Thomas Aquinas's” definition. That is defensible — it is the definition as the Christian tradition received it through Thomas — but the line should not imply he coined it.

**Scope, counted 2026-09-19** (five English renderings, one Latin): `chapter_02.md:103` “to will the good”; `chapter_02.md:191` “willing the good of another”; `chapter_05.md:67` the Latin and “to will the good of another”; `chapter_09.md:43` “to will the good of another”; `chapter_13.md:54` “willing the good.” Check the Preface, Introduction and Epilogue too.

**What it touches beyond wording.** Ch. 5 lines 69–73 parse the formula into two halves — “*the good*” (truth, justice, mercy) and “*for another*” (sacrifice). Dropping the article changes what that first half names, and *to* another rather than *for* or *of* another changes the second. Those lines, and `chapter_09.md:43` which recalls them, need rewriting together rather than a find-and-replace. Related: todo 43 (Ch. 9:43 inherits the *alicui*-carries-cost overreach fixed in Ch. 5) and todo 44 (sacrifice / self-gift) — the three should probably be settled in one sitting.

### 44. Sacrifice and self-gift — a deep dive on the two words, book-wide

*Opened 2026-09-19 at Patrick's request, at the close of the Ch. 5 pass.*

**The task, in his words:** do a deep dive into the differences between the word *sacrifice* and *self-gift*, to see whether we need to pivot or adjust the wording anywhere — in the definition or in the prose of the book.

**Why it is not a small question.** *Sacrifice* is one of the four pillars of the canonical definition, which is fixed word for word (“sacrifice,” never “sacrificial”; see §1). Any change to the definition itself is a decision of the first order and would touch every chapter, the Introduction's display setting, the Binding Check, and the website. *Self-gift* is St. John Paul II's language (*Gaudium et Spes* 24, “a sincere gift of himself”), which the book already leans on heavily, especially in Ch. 4. Ch. 9 carries both words in its title: “Sacrifice: Love's Eternal Self-Gift.”

**Questions to settle before proposing anything:** what each word carries that the other does not (cost and loss vs. donation and communion; the Temple and the Cross vs. the Trinity and marriage); whether *sacrifice* can be said of the inner life of the Trinity, where there is total gift but no loss — the book's own claim that love “originates in God” (Ch. 3) makes this the sharpest test; whether a lay reader hears *sacrifice* as grim deprivation in a way that undercuts the book's thesis; and whether the answer is a change to the definition, a one-time staging of the relationship between the two words (the entry 38 method), or no change at all.

**Scope, counted 2026-09-19:** forms of *sacrifice* appear about 570 times across the chapter files; *self-gift* or “gift of himself/ourselves” about 35 times, spread over twelve chapters (2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 17). The imbalance is itself part of the question.

**Method:** read, don't sweep. Inventory every use of both words across the manuscript first; sort them against the chapter text, not from a search result (see the entry 37 warning); then propose. Recent Ch. 5 context: sacrifice is what the *for another* costs (lines 71–73), and “a gift with strings attached calls itself sacrifice” (line 23) — both bear directly on this distinction.

### 30. Em-dash density pass (book-wide prose sweep)

*Opened 2026-09-04. Patrick's concern: heavy em-dash use has become a recognised marker of AI-generated text and invites ridicule. Agreed the concern is real; agreed the remedy below rather than a blanket character replacement.*

**⚠ What was considered and rejected.** The first instruction was to replace every em-dash with a hyphen book-wide. That was argued against and withdrawn, and the reasoning should not be re-litigated from scratch: (a) in printed books a hyphen standing where an em-dash belongs is the most reliable single mark of amateur typesetting, so it trades an AI-tell for a competence-tell in a manuscript going to a bishop and then to press; (b) 72 of the em-dashes are the `\hfill\small — Book C:V` Scripture-attribution convention the build consumes, and are not prose punctuation at all; (c) **the glyph is not the tell.** What reads as machine-written is the construction — a short declarative, a dash, then an appositive restating it with more feeling — repeated at high density. Swapping the character preserves the construction and loses the typography.

**Measured baseline (2026-09-04).** 2,579 em-dashes across the manuscript. 72 are Scripture attributions and stay out of scope. Worst case is `chapter_09.md` at 319 in roughly 2,400 words; then `chapter_15.md` 232, `chapter_11.md` 199, `chapter_06.md` 184, `chapter_10.md` 183, `chapter_07.md` 181. The Introduction has 43.

**The sweep.** Convert roughly a third to a half of the prose em-dashes into commas, colons, semicolons and full stops, keeping the em-dash where it does work no other mark can do. **The test, so it does not become mechanical:** an em-dash earns its place when it marks a genuine interruption, or a turn the sentence could not take with a comma. It does not earn its place when it merely joins a declarative to a restatement of itself — that is the construction to break up, and breaking it up improves the prose independently of how it reads to a machine-detector.

Do this as its own pass, after doctrinal work settles, and per chapter with a redline. Related: the four ornamental em-dashes around the three-line display of the canonical definition in `3_introduction.md` are handled separately in the Introduction redline.

### 28. Scripture verification tooling — adapted-quote sweep and reference validator

*Sidelined 2026-08-29 at Patrick's direction. Captured here in full so the next session does not have to re-derive it — especially the copyright constraint.*

**Why this exists.** The front matter no longer carries the sentence "Some quotations have been adapted or shortened for readability" (removed 2026-08-29, item 27), and the standing rule is now that Scripture is quoted in full and verbatim. That converts a disclaimer into a defect list: *any* adapted, shortened, or composited quotation still in the manuscript is now something the copyright notice contradicts. Every one must be restored to verbatim RSV or recast as an explicit paraphrase outside quotation marks.

**⚠ Hard constraint — do not download an "open source" RSV.** The RSV is *not* in the public domain. It is copyrighted 1946, 1952 and 1971 by the Division of Christian Education of the National Council of the Churches of Christ, and remains protected for decades. Any free RSV JSON or Bible-API mirror found online is a scrape, not a licensed release. Verifying this manuscript's Scripture against an unlicensed corpus would compromise the permissions position the book has just been put right on — a manuscript going to a bishop cannot have "checked against a pirated text" as the answer to how its quotations were verified.

**What the tooling can do with no copyrighted text at all** (working from a public-domain versification index — Douay-Rheims is the natural fit, being Catholic, public domain and inclusive of the deuterocanon):

- **Length-versus-range mismatch** — a nine-word quotation cited as spanning five verses is almost certainly shortened. Highest-yield adapted-quote detector, and it needs no RSV text.
- **Structural adaptation flags** — ellipses, bracketed insertions, quotations opening mid-sentence or lowercase, missing terminal punctuation, composite citations stitched from two locations.
- **Reference validation** — does the cited verse exist, are book names and ranges internally consistent, do any citations point at nothing.
- **Deduplicated quoted-verse count** — counting only verses whose text is reproduced, a partially quoted verse as one verse. **This closes Future Task \#26 outright.**
- **Drift report against `scripture-references.md`** — see the rebuild note below.

**What genuinely needs RSV text, and the legitimate ways to get it.** Only the flagged subset — expected to be a few dozen quotations, not the full ~400. At that size the options are all clean: Patrick reads them from his own RSV; exports them from Logos/Verbum/Accordance if RSV is licensed there; or requests an editorial text file from Friendship Press, which is already the party to contact if the verse count runs over 500 (item 26). Sourcing decision was not made — it was deferred with the rest of this item.

**Packaging.** Recommended shape: write and tune the script directly in the repo first, then wrap the working version as a reusable skill, since it will be rerun whenever chapters change. A cold subagent was considered and advised against — it would re-derive the chapter formatting conventions (intentional LaTeX, raw HTML blockquote divs, callout markup) and citation regexes that already exist in session context.

**Folded in: `scripture-references.md` needs a rebuild, not an edit.** That file is badly stale and cannot serve as the fair-use audit trail in its current state. It is built on the *pre-renumber* chapter structure — it lists "Chapter 11: Proof for the Existence of God" and stops at "Chapter 16: The Gospel," which is the numbering from before Prudence was inserted as the new Ch. 11. It logs 189 direct quotations against roughly 900 citations in the live chapters, names RSV-2CE 26 times, carries "Permission pending" language superseded by item 27, and its footer still reads "Last updated: \[Current Date\]." Its "Complete List of Unique Scripture References (Numbered for Fair Use Tracking)" — precisely the artifact item 26 requires — rests on that stale base. Regenerate it as script output rather than maintaining it by hand.

### 26. Formal RSV verse count for the copyright notice

The RSV gratis-use policy (National Council of Churches / Friendship Press) allows up to **500 verses** to be quoted without written permission or fee, provided the total is also less than one complete book of the Bible and less than 50% of the work's total words. The latter two conditions are comfortably satisfied — Matthew is the most-quoted book at roughly 105 of its 1,071 verses, and Scripture is a small fraction of the manuscript's word count. **The 500-verse condition is not yet settled.**

Scripted estimates on 2026-08-29 gave **391** verses on a strict count (quoted text immediately followed by its citation) and **681** on a loose count (which wrongly includes bare cross-references such as "see John 20:21–23" — those are not quotations and do not count toward the limit). The true figure lies between, and 500 sits inside that range.

**What is needed:** a verse-by-verse audit that counts only verses whose *text is actually reproduced*, counts a partially quoted verse as one verse, and de-duplicates verses quoted more than once. If the total exceeds 500, request a licence from Friendship Press before submission; if under, the notice now in `1_frontmatter.md` is sufficient on its own.

*Opened 2026-08-29, alongside the front-matter correction from RSV-2CE to RSV (see Completed).*
